input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-335: Machine Learning. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to both foundational and modern machine learning theories and algorithms, and their application in classification and regression. Topics include: Mathematical background of machine learning (e.g. statistical analysis and visualization of data), Bayesian decision theory, parametric and non-parameteric classification models (e.g., SVMs and Nearest Neighbor models) and neural network models (e.g. Convolutional, Recurrent, and Deep Neural Networks). Programming assignments are required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-335 and CSCI-635. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-335]
An introduction to both foundational and modern machine learning theories and algorithms, and their application in classification and regression. Topics include: Mathematical background of machine learning (e.g. statistical analysis and visualization of data), Bayesian decision theory, parametric and non-parameteric classification models (e.g., SVMs and Nearest Neighbor models) and neural network models (e.g. Convolutional, Recurrent, and Deep Neural Networks). Programming assignments are required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-335 and CSCI-635. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: Machine learning workflows systematically separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation to ensure reproducible results.
beats.example: A developer uses a pipeline to standardize features, train a classifier, and evaluate accuracy without mixing training and testing data.
beats.title: Introduction to Machine Learning Workflow
beats.visualDirection: Display a horizontal flowchart with six labeled nodes connected by arrows, representing the sequential workflow stages.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage, which invalidates model performance estimates.
beats.example: Scaling features using the mean and standard deviation calculated solely from the training set before splitting the data.
beats.title: Data Preparation and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Show a split diagram with 'Training Data' and 'Test Data' boxes, highlighting that preprocessing parameters are derived exclusively from the training box.

beats.claim: Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels.
beats.example: Classifying email as spam or ham uses labeled data, whereas clustering customers by purchasing behavior uses unlabeled data.
beats.title: Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning
beats.visualDirection: Present two side-by-side icons: a labeled dataset with a target column for supervised learning, and a scatter plot of unlabeled points for unsupervised learning.

beats.claim: The mathematical background of machine learning relies on statistical analysis and visualization of data to understand distributions and relationships.
beats.example: Plotting a histogram and box plot to detect outliers and skewness before selecting a regression model.
beats.title: Statistical Analysis and Data Visualization
beats.visualDirection: Render a composite image showing a histogram, a box plot, and a scatter plot with a regression line, each labeled with its statistical purpose.

beats.claim: Bayesian decision theory provides a probabilistic framework for making predictions by updating beliefs based on observed evidence and prior knowledge.
beats.example: Calculating the posterior probability of a medical diagnosis given a test result, using prior prevalence and test sensitivity/specificity.
beats.title: Bayesian Decision Theory
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a Bayesian update cycle with three boxes: Prior, Likelihood, and Posterior, connected by arrows showing probability adjustment.

beats.claim: Parametric classification models, such as Support Vector Machines, learn decision boundaries by optimizing parameters that maximize the margin between classes.
beats.example: Training an SVM on a dataset of handwritten digits to draw a hyperplane that separates correct from incorrect digit classifications.
beats.title: Parametric Classification Models
beats.visualDirection: Draw a 2D scatter plot with a straight decision boundary line, highlighting the margin distance between the boundary and the nearest data points.

beats.claim: Non-parametric classification models, such as Nearest Neighbor algorithms, make predictions based on the similarity of new instances to existing training examples without assuming
beats.example: Assigning a new customer to a segment by finding the three closest historical customers in feature space and taking their majority class.
beats.title: Non-Parametric Classification Models
beats.visualDirection: Show a 2D plot with a query point surrounded by a circle, highlighting the three nearest training points and their assigned labels.

beats.claim: Neural network models, including Convolutional, Recurrent, and Deep Neural Networks, process complex data structures through layered transformations to learn hierarchical features.
beats.example: Using a Convolutional Neural Network to detect edges and textures in images, or a Recurrent Neural Network to predict the next word in a sentence sequence.
beats.title: Neural Network Architectures
beats.visualDirection: Display a simplified diagram of a three-layer neural network with input, hidden, and output nodes, showing weighted connections and activation functions.

beats.claim: Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors, and hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation to prevent overfitting.
beats.example: Using precision and recall for imbalanced classification tasks, and tuning learning rate via cross-validation before testing on held-out data.
beats.title: Model Evaluation and Hyperparameter Selection
beats.visualDirection: Show a confusion matrix and a learning curve graph, with annotations indicating metric selection and cross-validation folds.

beats.claim: A practical analysis checklist ensures robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness by verifying data quality, monitoring context changes, and aligning model behavior
beats.example: Before deployment, verify that preprocessing parameters were not fitted on test data, check for bias in predictions across demographic groups, and schedule post-deployment monitoring.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a five-item checklist with checkboxes: Data Quality Verified, Leakage Prevented, Metrics Matched, Fairness Audited, Monitoring Scheduled.

With the foundation in place, examine how Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning operates in a concrete sequence. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels.
